80696.subject: How to actually make money this bull market (and keep it)

Adrian's DeFi Insights 

Автор: Adrian Pape

Last cycle I was early on Solana, farmed Hyperliquid before its airdrop and caught the AI narrative before it went mainstream. I still left a lot of money on the table. Not because of bad analysis but because I had no written plan for what to do once I was right, or wrong. Here’s the framework I use now, a first look at my own plan, and a prompt that walks you through building yours. Take your time, this is the most important process to make it in this bull market. Why a plan matters A trading plan decides more than when you buy. It sets how big a position can get, what makes you add or cut, and when the original idea stops being valid. You need it most when the market does something you didn’t expect. Without one, you make the hardest decisions on a red candle with your phone in one hand on the toilet (nobody has ever sized a position well in that setting). With a trading plan, you set the rules while calm. When a trigger hits, you look up what you already decided. What mine looks like (a preview) My own plan runs to 13 sections. I’m publishing the full version next week. Here’s the skeleton: Leverage is still in there. The difference from last cycle is that it now has written conditions for going up and a hard rule for getting out. The open-items list is the part I’d copy first. Once you write down what you haven’t decided yet, you stop deciding it at the worst possible moment. How to build yours (8 steps) 1. Set your goal and time horizon Answer three questions: What am I trying to achieve? With how much capital? Over what period? “I want to make as much as possible” helps with zero decisions later. This works better: “I want to build capital over several years and can accept a portfolio drawdown of up to X USD.” Your horizon decides which information matters. If you hold for months, a 4-hour candle is noise. If you trade short-term, you need tighter rules and more frequent checks. Then check that goal, timeframe and required return fit together. If the goal only works with high leverage, write that leverage into the plan as a risk. 2. Write down where you actually stand Fill this in before you plan any entry: Watch for hidden correlation. Welcome back! Claude shipped a feature that works while you sleep and something users weren’t told about, NVIDIA built a reconstruction system that audits itself, and Satya Nadella wants an emergency brake on every model.  In today's Atlas Newsletter: title: text Claude is running things you can’t see: One release Anthropic announced, and one users found by testing what Opus 5.5 shouldn’t know. NVIDIA researchers introduced GATOR: Casual photos in, simulation-ready 3D assets out, with an agent that edits its own meshes in Blender. A Claude skill that explains ideas by building them: Ask about a cache key and it invents a pin-tumbler lock you can take apart. Microsoft’s CEO says treat AI like a risky employee: Nadella’s rule: assume a model is compromised, then design around it. PS: Want to collaborate with the biggest GTM engine and distribution moat for AI companies? You can feature your tool with us and reach millions. Claude is running things you can't see Two things happened to Claude this week. One Anthropic announced. Every Pro and Max user on the waitlist now has Claude Code Projects.  You give Claude one ongoing goal and it splits the work into separate tasks, each running on its own in the background.  They keep going after you close your laptop, and you can check in from your phone. Each task can open code changes on GitHub and fix them when tests fail.  It carries memory across tasks, and it handles non-code work too, like reading a pile of support tickets for the most common problems.  It also burns through usage limits faster than regular Claude Code. The other thing, Anthropic hasn't said a word about. Users are convinced Opus 5.5 is being answered by a newer model. The test going around asks it about a recent benchmark it shouldn't know without searching. If it knows, people say you got the new one. TestingCatalog found a hidden item codenamed Arborio that looks like a Claude Health page for the web, a feature currently mobile-only in the US. Another, codenamed Iggy, shows nothing but a sun icon.  One guest at a New York AI dinner reported the room's consensus: Fable 5.5 will be stunning, and OpenAI will beat it in December with a model called Bel. Handing specific tasks to AI models will often make sense: they are much better than humans at many things. But AI's range of capabilities, allied to a convenient conversational interface and a seductively confident persona, raises the prospect less of delegation than of wholesale capitulation. Earlier this year I wrote a column about the risks of cognitive surrender to AI. Anxiety has only grown since.  My weekly newsletter for subscribers reveals the tiny workplace triumphs that recipients are proudest of. You can sign up here.  Andrew Palmer, Bartleby columnist Editor’s pick AI and the danger of cognitive surrender  How much should managers let bots do the thinking? Calculators didn’t make everyone innumerate. GPS navigation systems made driving easier. In any conversation about the cognitive effects of artificial intelligence, these two earlier technologies are reasonably likely to come up. Each is a useful entry-point into two big questions. How might AI change the way people think, and should managers do anything in response? From the Boss Class vault Presentations: It’s all in the knees How to captivate a room full of people To many workers the idea of presenting to a room of colleagues is nightmarish. Stumbling, umming and rambling is hard for the listener and nerve-racking for the speaker. Michael Chad Hoeppner is an actor-turned-presentation coach. On our “Boss Class” podcast the author of “Don’t Say Um” explains how an unusual technique might help presenters stay cool. Elsewhere in The Economist ▸ A no-rules approach to AI is mad politics and worse policy  ▸ The rise of the AI marketplace  ▸ Indian manufacturing’s moment may finally have arrived  Enjoying this newsletter? If you’re a subscriber you can get it in your inbox every Monday by signing up here. You’ll get more on work and office life from our management columnist.
